Quiz 1: Non-Parametric Tests ✓ Done

  
    Question 1: When should you use a Wilcoxon test instead of a t-test?
    When the data is not normally distributed
    When you have more than 1000 data points
    When comparing more than 2 groups
    
  
  
    Question 2: The Wilcoxon test operates on the...
    Raw values, exactly like the t-test
    Ranks of the values, not the raw values themselves
    Squared differences between values
    
  
  
    Question 3: In the plenum's by-hand computation, the U statistic (U = R1 - n1(n1+1)/2) is derived from...
    The sum of ranks (R1) of one group, corrected for the group's own size
    The mean of the raw values
    The standard deviation of the combined sample
    
  
  CHECK ANSWERS
  




Quiz 2: Proportion Tests ✓ Done

  
    Question 1: What kind of question are proportion tests (Fisher / chi-square) designed to answer?
    Whether the means of two continuous variables differ
    Whether there is a significant relationship between two categorical variables
    Whether a dataset follows a normal distribution
    
  
  
    Question 2: An odds-ratio (OR) of exactly 1 in a 2×2 contingency table means...
    There is no association between the two categorical variables
    There is a perfect positive association
    The test cannot be run
    
  
  
    Question 3: The chi-square test statistic compares which two things?
    The observed counts in the contingency table vs. the counts expected if there were no relationship
    Two means
    Two standard deviations
    
  
  CHECK ANSWERS
  




Quiz 3: Power of a Test ✓ Done

  
    Question 1: In the biomarker diagnostic example, what does β (the Type II error rate) represent?
    The false-positive rate — diagnosing a healthy patient as sick
    The false-negative rate — failing to detect the condition in a patient who actually has it
    The proportion of patients tested
    
  
  
    Question 2: The power of a test is defined as...
    α, the significance level
    1 − β, the probability of correctly detecting a real effect
    The sample mean
    
  
  
    Question 3: Which of the following would increase the power of the diagnostic test in the example?
    Taking fewer measurements per patient (smaller n)
    Taking more measurements per patient (larger n), which shrinks the standard error
    Ignoring the significance level entirely
    
  
  CHECK ANSWERS
  




Quiz 4: False Positives, False Negatives & FDR (Plenum) ✓ Done

  
    Question 1: When H0 is actually true, what should the distribution of p-values look like across many repeated tests?
    Uniformly distributed between 0 and 1
    Always exactly 0.05
    Concentrated near 0
    
  
  
    Question 2: In the plenum's gene expression simulation (900 genes with no real difference, 100 genes with a real difference), what does the False Discovery Rate (FDR) measure?
    The proportion of all 1000 genes that are truly different
    The proportion of genes called "significant" (test-positive) that are actually false positives
    The total number of genes tested
    
  
  
    Question 3: Why does the FPR (false-positive rate) stop equaling α when the data is not normally distributed and you still use a t-test?
    Because the t-test's theoretical guarantees rely on the normality assumption, which is violated
    Because R computes p-values incorrectly for non-normal data
    α always equals the FPR no matter what
    
  
  CHECK ANSWERS

Use the language toggle above to select R or Python, then work through the quizzes below.




Quiz 1: The Central Limit Theorem ✓ Done

  
    Question 1: In the coffee shop example, individual waiting times follow a right-skewed Gamma distribution. What does the Central Limit Theorem say about the distribution of sample means of waiting times as the sample size n grows?
    It stays right-skewed, just like the individual waiting times
    It becomes approximately normal, regardless of the shape of the original distribution
    It becomes uniform
    
  
  
    Question 2: What is one essential condition for the Central Limit Theorem to hold?
    The original variable must already be normally distributed
    The individual random variables being averaged must be independent of each other
    The sample size must be exactly 30
    
  
  
    Question 3: Looking at the Q-Q plots for n = 2, n = 10 and n = 200 sample means, what pattern do you see?
    The fit to the normal line gets worse as n increases
    The fit to the normal line gets better as n increases, becoming almost perfect at n = 200
    n has no effect on the Q-Q plot
    
  
  CHECK ANSWERS
  




Quiz 2: Standard Error & Sample Size ✓ Done

  
    Question 1: What does the formula SE = σ / √n tell you?
    The standard error shrinks as the sample size n grows
    The standard error grows as the sample size n grows
    The standard error is independent of n
    
  
  
    Question 2: The exercise notes "diminishing returns": going from n=10 to n=20 helps more than going from n=80 to n=90. Why?
    Because SE depends on √n, so each additional observation reduces SE less and less at larger n
    Because R has a bug for large sample sizes
    Because the mean changes at large n
    
  
  
    Question 3: Does the mean of the sample means change as the sample size n increases?
    No — it stays centered on the true population mean; only the spread (SE) shrinks
    Yes — it increases proportionally with n
    Yes — it decreases proportionally with n
    
  
  CHECK ANSWERS
  




Quiz 3: Confidence Intervals ✓ Done

  
    Question 1: What does a "95% confidence interval" mean?
    There is a 95% probability that any single observation falls in this range
    If we repeated the sampling many times, about 95% of the constructed intervals would contain the true population parameter
    The sample mean is wrong 95% of the time
    
  
  
    Question 2: In the coffee-cup example (n = 9 cups), why do we use the t-distribution with 8 degrees of freedom rather than the normal distribution to compute the critical value?
    Because the sample size is small, and the true standard deviation is unknown and estimated from the sample
    Because coffee cup volumes are always t-distributed
    Because degrees of freedom only apply to normal distributions
    
  
  
    Question 3: Comparing a 90% CI and a 95% CI computed from the same data, which one is wider?
    The 90% CI is wider
    The 95% CI is wider — higher confidence requires a larger margin
    They are always exactly the same width
    
  
  CHECK ANSWERS
  




Quiz 4: Plenum Demos — CLT in Action ✓ Done

  
    Question 1: In the dice-sum ("Augensumme") plenum demo, rolling 2 dice and averaging over N repeated pairs of rolls, what happens to the distribution of the averaged sum as N grows from 1 to 100?
    It stays exactly the same, uniformly spread between 2 and 12
    It becomes increasingly concentrated and bell-shaped around the theoretical mean of 7
    It becomes more spread out and skewed
    
  
  
    Question 2: In the chocolate-bar weight demo, individual error sources (weighing cocoa, weighing sugar, ...) are each uniformly distributed on [-1, 1]. What happens to the distribution of the total error once you sum up 100 such independent uniform error sources?
    It stays uniformly distributed, just wider
    It becomes approximately normally distributed — confirmed by the Q-Q plot lying on the diagonal
    It becomes a Poisson distribution
    
  
  
    Question 3: The plenum repeats the "mean of N samples" experiment starting from Normal, Poisson and t-distributed data. What is the common conclusion across all of them?
    Only data that starts out normal ends up with normal sample means
    Regardless of the starting distribution, the sample means concentrate around the true mean with a spread shrinking like 1/√N — the CLT in action
    The sample mean is unrelated to the true mean
    
  
  CHECK ANSWERS

Use the language toggle above to select R or Python, then work through the quizzes below.




Quiz 1: Hierarchical Clustering ✓ Done

  
    Question 1: What is the key difference between k-means and hierarchical clustering?
    They are mathematically identical, just different function names
    K-means requires the number of clusters upfront; hierarchical clustering builds a dendrogram you can cut at any level afterwards
    Hierarchical clustering can only be used on 2 variables at a time
    
  
  
    Question 2: What property must a distance matrix always have, e.g. for use in pheatmap()?
    It must be symmetrical — the distance from A to B equals the distance from B to A
    It must only contain values between 0 and 1
    It must be based on Euclidean distance only
    
  
  
    Question 3: Why do we often select only the top 25% most variable genes before clustering samples?
    To reduce file size only, it has no effect on the analysis
    Low-variance genes barely differ between samples, so they add mostly noise rather than useful signal
    pheatmap() cannot handle more than 100 rows
    
  
  CHECK ANSWERS
  




Quiz 2: Principal Component Analysis (PCA) ✓ Done

  
    Question 1: What is the main goal of PCA?
    To remove every correlated variable from the dataset
    To reduce dimensionality by finding new, uncorrelated variables (principal components) that capture as much variance as possible
    To impute missing values automatically
    
  
  
    Question 2: In prcomp(bc_data, center = TRUE, scale = TRUE), why do we scale the data?
    Scaling is mandatory syntax with no statistical purpose
    So variables measured on larger numeric scales don't dominate the PCA just because of their range
    So the data gets converted to ranks, like Spearman correlation
    
  
  
    Question 3: What does a scree plot show?
    The pairwise correlation between all original variables
    How much variance each principal component explains, usually shown in decreasing order
    The cluster assignment of each patient
    
  
  CHECK ANSWERS
  




Quiz 3: Putting it together ✓ Done

  
    Question 1: In the PCA loadings (pca_result$rotation), what does a large positive value for a variable on PC1 mean?
    That variable has too many missing values
    That variable contributes strongly and positively to PC1
    That variable is uncorrelated with everything else
    
  
  
    Question 2: How can PCA be combined with k-means clustering?
    They cannot be combined
    Run k-means on the first few principal components (pca$x) instead of the original variables
    PCA replaces the need for clustering entirely
    
  
  
    Question 3: What is one key difference between what hierarchical clustering and PCA each produce?
    Hierarchical clustering produces a dendrogram/tree of similarity; PCA produces new continuous axes (components) that summarize variance
    They always produce exactly the same plot
    PCA only works on categorical data, clustering does not
    
  
  CHECK ANSWERS

text:
Programming Languages and Their Working Environments
Before we start, it is important to understand the difference between the programming language itself and the program in which we write.

1. The Language: R and Python
R and Python are the “engines” behind your analysis. For your computer to understand what you want from it, you need to download the language as base software.

Python: Installed as a program from python.org.
R: Installed as “Base R” from the CRAN network.

2. The Tool: The IDE (RStudio & VS Code)

What Do You Need for Setup?
If you later want to work on your own computer, this is the correct order:

Install the engine: Download Python or R (provides the “language”).
Set up the workspace: Install an IDE like RStudio or VS Code (your workstation).
Unpack the tools: Install so-called “packages” within the IDE. These are extensions for specific tasks, such as drawing biological diagrams.







TipOur Tip for Getting Started



To watch videos, follow the course and take quizzes, no installation is required. However, to work through the practical markdown files, you will need RStudio (for R) or VS Code (for Python) installed on your computer. We recommend setting this up early — these tools will be your daily companions throughout the course.

title: Orientation in This Course
text:
Working with Markdown
In this course we do not use ordinary text documents or pure program code. In addition to this website, we work with Markdown files as an offline alternative.
In science, reproducibility (traceability) is crucial. Markdown allows us to do so-called Literate Programming: * We write our text (explanations, hypotheses). * We embed the actual code (R or Python) directly within it. * We let the computer render the document (in RStudio often via the Knit button).
The result is a finished document (HTML, PDF, or Word) in which the text, the code, and the resulting graphics are perfectly combined.

The Structure of a File

The text: Regular text with simple formatting (**bold**, *italic*, # Heading).
The code chunks: Blocks that begin with three backticks. This is where the actual code is executed. It is recommended to name each chunk — this keeps your document tidy and greatly facilitates troubleshooting.
The YAML header: The area at the very top between the --- lines for title and author.








NoteLanguage-Specific Introduction



Depending on whether you have switched to “R” or “Python” above, you will now see a more detailed introduction to the respective environment below.

title: Orientation in This Course
text:
Focus: R and RStudio
R is a powerful language for statistical data analysis. We recommend that you also take the introductory courses at DataCamp to get a feel for the syntax. RStudio is an “Integrated Development Environment” (IDE) that helps you write code, visualize data, and save results.

The RStudio Interface
The interface is divided into four main areas:

Source (top left): This is where you write your scripts and Markdown files. To create a new file, click on the New File icon (green plus) at the top left. Everything written here can be saved.
Console (bottom left): Code is executed immediately here. For example, type 3 + 4 and press Enter — the result appears immediately. The console is ideal for commands that you do not need to save permanently.
Environment (top right): All variables, lists, and datasets that you have created and defined during your session are displayed here.
Files/Plots/Help (bottom right): Here you manage your files, view generated graphics, or search the help for functions (e.g., with ?matrix).




The main areas of RStudio




First Steps in Programming

Assignments: Values are loaded into variables with <- or = (e.g., a <- 10). The variable then appears in the Environment.
R as a calculator: R is excellent for mathematical calculations. You can calculate directly with variables:

#| '!! shinylive warning !!': |
#|   shinylive does not work in self-contained HTML documents.
#|   Please set `embed-resources: false` in your metadata.
#| standalone: true
#| viewerHeight: 300
library(shiny)
ui <- fluidPage(
  textAreaInput("code", "R Chunk: Mathematical Operations", value = "x <- 5\ny <- 3\nSum <- x + y\nSum * 5", width = '100%', height = '100px'),
  actionButton("run", "Run Code", class = "btn-success"),
  verbatimTextOutput("out")
)
server <- function(input, output) {
  observeEvent(input$run, { output$out <- renderPrint({ eval(parse(text = input$code)) }) })
}
shinyApp(ui, server)

Case Sensitivity: R is extremely picky. hello is a different variable from Hello.
Getting help: Use the documentation directly in RStudio or online resources:

guru99 R Tutorial
Babraham Bioinformatics
R for Data Science

Workspace: Use ls() to list your variables and rm(a) to delete them — Caution: rm() deletes irreversibly, so use it carefully! Your entire environment can be saved as an .RData file and restored in a later session with load("MyEnvironment.RData").
Working Directory: Via the Files -> More -> Set As Working Directory tab, you define which folder R should look in for your files.


Helpful Tips in the Editor

Autocomplete: In RStudio, quotation marks "" and brackets () usually appear automatically in pairs. This helps you avoid syntax errors caused by forgotten characters.
History: Using the arrow keys (up/down) you can scroll through your most recently used commands in the console.
Comments: Everything after a # is ignored by R. Use this generously to explain your code to yourself and others.



Variables & Assignments
We can load values (numbers or text) into variables. In R, the arrow <- is traditionally used for this, but = is also possible.
#| '!! shinylive warning !!': |
#|   shinylive does not work in self-contained HTML documents.
#|   Please set `embed-resources: false` in your metadata.
#| standalone: true
#| viewerHeight: 300
library(shiny)
ui <- fluidPage(
  textAreaInput("code", "R Chunk: Variables & Assignments", value = "a <- \"Hello world!\"\nhello = \"Hello world!\"\nprint(a)\nprint(hello)", width = '100%', height = '120px'),
  actionButton("run", "Run Code", class = "btn-success"),
  verbatimTextOutput("out")
)
server <- function(input, output) {
  observeEvent(input$run, { output$out <- renderPrint({ eval(parse(text = input$code)) }) })
}
shinyApp(ui, server)

title: Orientation in This Course
text:
Python and VS Code
Python is a versatile and widely used programming language that is particularly well-suited for data analysis, machine learning, and scientific computing. We recommend that you also take the introductory courses at DataCamp to get a feel for the syntax. VS Code is a flexible development environment (IDE) that can be optimally adapted for Python through extensions.

The VS Code Interface
The interface is divided into four main areas:

Editor (center): This is where you write your scripts and notebooks. To create a new file, click on the New File icon at the top left in the Explorer. Everything written here can be saved. The file extensions determine in which programming language you are writing and how the file can be used (.py/.ipynb for Python, .r for R, .md for Markdown).
Terminal (bottom): Code is executed immediately here and files can be launched. Connections to clusters, communication with GitHub, or searching for files also work via the terminal. The terminal can be opened, for example, at the top right (3rd icon from the right).
Explorer (left): Here you manage your files and folders. These are either stored locally on your computer or on a cluster.
Control Center (far left): Here you can, for example, search documents for a keyword, connect and manage GitHub repositories, debug, install extensions, and manage remote connections (e.g., clusters).




The main areas of VS Code




First Steps in Programming

Assignments: In Python, values are loaded into variables with = (e.g., a = 10). Unlike R, there is no <- in Python.
Python as a calculator: Python is excellent for mathematical calculations. You can calculate directly with variables:

#| '!! shinylive warning !!': |
#|   shinylive does not work in self-contained HTML documents.
#|   Please set `embed-resources: false` in your metadata.
#| standalone: true
#| viewerHeight: 300
from shiny import App, ui, render, reactive
import io, contextlib

app_ui = ui.page_fluid(
    ui.input_text_area("code", "Python Chunk: Mathematical Operations", value="x = 5\ny = 3\nSum = x + y\nprint(Sum * 5)", width='100%', height='100px'),
    ui.input_action_button("run", "Run Code", class_="btn-success"),
    ui.output_text_verbatim("out")
)

def server(input, output, session):
    @render.text
    @reactive.event(input.run)
    def out():
        f = io.StringIO()
        with contextlib.redirect_stdout(f):
            exec(input.code(), {})
        return f.getvalue()

app = App(app_ui, server)

Case Sensitivity: Python is just as picky as R. hello is a different variable from Hello.



Getting Help:
Use the documentation directly in VS Code or online resources: Python Documentation W3Schools Python Tutorial Python for Data Science Handbook

Workspace: Use dir() to list all current variables and objects, and del a to delete a variable — Caution: del deletes irreversibly, so use it carefully!
Working Directory: With import os and os.getcwd() you can display the current directory; with os.chdir("path/to/folder") you change it.



Helpful Tips in the Editor

Autocomplete: VS Code automatically suggests functions, variable names, and brackets. Quotation marks "" and brackets () often appear automatically in pairs — this helps avoid syntax errors.
History: In the terminal you can scroll through your most recently used commands using the arrow keys (up/down).
Comments: Everything after a # is ignored by Python — just like in R. Use comments generously to explain your code.



Variables & Assignments
We can load values (numbers or text) into variables. In Python, = is used exclusively for assignments.
#| '!! shinylive warning !!': |
#|   shinylive does not work in self-contained HTML documents.
#|   Please set `embed-resources: false` in your metadata.
#| standalone: true
#| viewerHeight: 300
from shiny import App, ui, render, reactive
import io, contextlib

app_ui = ui.page_fluid(
    ui.input_text_area("code", "Python Chunk: Variables & Assignments", value='a = "Hello world!"\nhello = "Hello world!"\nprint(a)\nprint(hello)', width='100%', height='120px'),
    ui.input_action_button("run", "Run Code", class_="btn-success"),
    ui.output_text_verbatim("out")
)

def server(input, output, session):
    @render.text
    @reactive.event(input.run)
    def out():
        f = io.StringIO()
        with contextlib.redirect_stdout(f):
            exec(input.code(), {})
        return f.getvalue()

app = App(app_ui, server)

Quiz 1: Correlation ✓ Done

  
    Question 1: What is the main difference between Pearson and Spearman correlation?
    They always return the exact same value
    Pearson measures the linear relationship using raw values; Spearman uses ranks to measure monotonic relationships
    Pearson only works on categorical variables
    
  
  
    Question 2: What does cor(dat$stab.glu, dat$glyhb, method='pearson') compute?
    The Pearson correlation coefficient between the two variables
    The p-value of a t-test comparing the two variables
    The mean difference between the two variables
    
  
  
    Question 3: Why is Spearman correlation often more robust to outliers than Pearson?
    It automatically removes missing values
    It is based on ranks rather than raw values, so extreme values shift the ranks only slightly
    It only works with normally distributed data
    
  
  CHECK ANSWERS
  




Quiz 2: Missing Data ✓ Done

  
    Question 1: Given rmv.rows <- apply(dat, 1, function(x) sum(is.na(x))), what does i.missing <- which(rmv.rows > 0) contain?

    The row indices of patients that have at least one missing value
    The column names that contain missing values
    
  
  
    Question 2: Why do we usually handle missing values before computing correlations or running k-means?
    R cannot store NA in a dataframe at all
    Functions like cor() or kmeans() cannot handle NAs and will fail or return NA
    Missing values always mean the whole row was measured incorrectly
    
  
  
    Question 3: What does dat[-i.missing, ] do?
    Keeps only the rows with missing values
    Removes the rows with missing values, keeping everyone else
    Removes the columns with missing values
    
  
  CHECK ANSWERS
  




Quiz 3: Introduction to Clustering ✓ Done

  
    Question 1: What does "unsupervised" mean in unsupervised learning?
    The analysis needs no data at all
    There are no known group labels — the method finds structure purely from the data itself
    A human manually assigns every observation to a group first
    
  
  
    Question 2: What is the general goal of clustering?
    Predict a continuous outcome variable from other variables
    Group similar observations together while separating the dissimilar ones
    Remove all missing values from a dataset
    
  
  
    Question 3: In the gene expression example (brca.exp, genes × samples), what are we clustering when we run kmeans(x = t(brca.exp), ...)?
    The genes (rows)
    The samples/patients (columns) — that's why the matrix is transposed with t()
    The p-values of a statistical test
    
  
  CHECK ANSWERS
  




Quiz 4: K-means Clustering ✓ Done

  
    Question 1: In kmeans(x, centers = k, nstart = 10), what does centers control?
    The number of clusters requested
    The number of random restarts
    The distance metric used
    
  
  
    Question 2: What does the Within Sum of Squares (WSS, km$tot.withinss) measure?
    How spread out the entire dataset is, regardless of clustering
    How compact each cluster is — lower WSS means tighter clusters
    The number of points assigned to each cluster
    
  
  
    Question 3: Why does WSS always decrease as you increase the number of clusters k?
    Because kmeans() recalculates the data randomly each time
    Because with more clusters, points sit closer to their own centroid — down to zero once every point is its own cluster
    Because R ignores clusters beyond k = 5
    
  
  CHECK ANSWERS
  




Quiz 5: Plenum Recap — Correlation & Clustering Deep Dive ✓ Done

  
    Question 1: In the plenum, a single outlier point was added to a strong linear relationship and moved further and further away. What happened to the Pearson and Spearman correlations?
    Both stayed exactly the same
    The Pearson correlation kept changing as the outlier moved further away, while the Spearman correlation stayed constant — because moving the point further doesn't change its rank
    The Spearman correlation kept changing while Pearson stayed constant
    
  
  
    Question 2: The plenum simulated points scattered randomly in a circle (no real cluster structure) and ran k-means with centers = 2 25 times with different random initializations. What did this demonstrate?

    When there is no real cluster structure in the data, the k-means result can differ a lot depending on the random initialization
    K-means cannot be run more than once on the same dataset
    
  
  
    Question 3: The plenum compared standard k-means (Euclidean distance) with a custom "k-medians" implementation using Manhattan distance on the same 6 points. What does this comparison illustrate?
    Manhattan and Euclidean distance always produce identical clusters
    The choice of distance metric (and center type: mean vs. median) can change which points end up in which cluster
    Manhattan distance can only be used for time-series data
    
  
  CHECK ANSWERS

    Question 2: A footballer scores 90% of penalties (p = 0.9) and takes 20 in training (L = 20). Using E(X) = L·p, the expected number of goals is 18. What do L and p represent in the binomial distribution?

    L = number of successes, p = number of trials

    Question 3: What does the negative binomial distribution describe?
    The probability of exactly k successes in a fixed number of trials
    The number of failures (or trials) needed to reach a fixed number of successes r
    The probability that a continuous variable falls below a threshold
    
  
  CHECK ANSWERS
  




Quiz 3: Poisson Distribution ✓ Done

  
    Question 1: The Poisson distribution has a single parameter λ, with E(X) = Var(X) = λ. In the gene mutation example, what did λ represent?

    The average (expected) number of mutations accumulated after one generation
    The total number of genes in the genome
    
  
  
    Question 2: What does ppois(q = 10, lambda = 30) compute?
    The probability of observing exactly 10 events
    The probability of observing 10 or fewer events, given an average rate of 30

    Question 3: On average 50 students attend a lecture. Which function computes the probability that exactly 60 students show up?

    ppois(60, lambda = 50)
    rpois(60, lambda = 50)
    
  
  CHECK ANSWERS
  




Quiz 4: Normal & t-Distribution ✓ Done

  
    Question 1: In the TP53 gene expression example, why can we use the sample mean and standard deviation from 586 patients as mu and sigma of a normal distribution model?

    Question 2: What makes the standard normal distribution special?
    It has mean = 0 and standard deviation = 1
    It only applies to sample sizes below 30

    Question 3: What happens to the t-distribution as the degrees of freedom increase?
    Its tails get wider and wider
    It converges towards the standard normal distribution
    It becomes a Poisson distribution
    
  
  CHECK ANSWERS
  




Quiz 5: Relationships Between Distributions (Plenum) ✓ Done

  
    Question 1: Under what condition does the Poisson distribution become approximately equivalent to a Normal distribution?
    When λ is large (λ ≫ 1)
    When λ = 0
    Only for discrete data
    
  
  
    Question 2: A Binomial(n, p) distribution converges to a Poisson(λ = np) distribution under which condition?
    When p = 0.5 exactly
    When the number of trials n → ∞ while n·p stays constant (equal to λ)
    Never — Binomial and Poisson are unrelated
    
  
  
    Question 3: In a Q-Q plot comparing quantiles from two distributions, what does it mean when the points fall closely along the diagonal line?
    The two distributions are unrelated
    The two distributions are very similar to each other
    One distribution has twice the variance of the other

title: Basics in Coding
text: This page is a quick-reference for the coding basics covered in Week 1. Keep it open in a browser tab while working through the markdowns. Use the language toggle above to switch between R and Python.

title: Basics in Coding
text:
Variables & Assignments

Assigning values
Use <- or = to assign a value to a variable. R is case-sensitive — hello and Hello are different objects.
a   <- 2            # numeric
b   <- TRUE         # logical
name <- "Rosalinde" # character (string)

a + 3               # use in calculations: returns 5
print(name)         # explicitly print to console



Function
What it does


str(x)
Show structure and type of x


ls()
List all objects in the environment


rm(x)
Remove variable x from the environment


load("file.RData")
Reload a saved environment

title: Basics in Coding
text:
Vectors

Creating & accessing vectors
A vector is a sequence of values of the same type. When you mix types, R converts everything to the lowest common type (logical → numeric → character).
y <- c(9, 3, 7, 2)   # numeric vector of length 4
length(y)             # 4

# Indexing
y[3]          # 7        — third element
y[2:4]        # 3 7 2    — elements 2 to 4
y[-2]         # 9 7 2    — all except element 2
y[y < 5]      # 3 2      — elements where condition is TRUE

# Logical tests (applied to each element)
y < 5         # FALSE TRUE FALSE TRUE
sum(y < 5)    # 2  — count of elements satisfying condition

# Modifying
y[1] <- 10    # replace first element

  TRUE / FALSE in arithmetic: R treats TRUE as 1 and FALSE as 0.
  So sum(c(TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, TRUE)) = 3 — a quick way to count matching elements.

title: Basics in Coding
text:
Matrices

Creating & accessing matrices
A matrix is a 2-dimensional structure. All elements must be the same type. Indexing uses [row, column] — leave one side empty to select all.
X <- matrix(1:6, nrow = 2, ncol = 3, byrow = TRUE)
#      [,1] [,2] [,3]
# [1,]    1    2    3
# [2,]    4    5    6

dim(X)        # c(2, 3)  — rows, then columns
X[1, 2]       # 2        — row 1, column 2
X[2, ]        # 4 5 6    — entire second row
X[, 1]        # 1 4      — entire first column

# Building from vectors
A <- cbind(c(1,2), c(3,4), c(5,6))   # join as columns
B <- rbind(c(1,2,3), c(4,5,6))       # join as rows

# Naming
rownames(A) <- c("r1", "r2")
colnames(A) <- c("p1", "p2", "p3")



Function
What it does


dim(X)
Returns c(rows, columns)


nrow(X) / ncol(X)
Number of rows / columns


cbind(x, y)
Combine vectors as columns


rbind(x, y)
Combine vectors as rows


colnames(X)
Get or set column names


rownames(X)
Get or set row names

title: Basics in Coding
text:
Lists

Creating & accessing lists
Lists can hold elements of different types and lengths — unlike vectors or matrices. Access elements with $name or [[ ]].
L <- list(color = c("blue", "red"), size = 5, active = TRUE)

# Accessing content (returns the actual value)
L$color           # "blue" "red"
L[["color"]]      # same — "blue" "red"
L[["color"]][2]   # "red"

# Single brackets return a list, not the content
L["color"]        # a list of length 1 (not the vector!)
length(L["color"])   # 1
length(L[["color"]]) # 2

# Modifying & deleting
L[["size"]] <- 10     # change an element
L[["new"]]  <- "hi"   # add a new element
L[[3]] <- NULL         # delete third element

  [ ] vs [[ ]]: Single brackets always return a list.
  Double brackets return the content. Use [[ ]] when you want to work with the value.

title: Basics in Coding
text:
Dataframes

Creating & accessing dataframes
A dataframe is like a table: rows are observations, columns are variables. Unlike matrices, different columns can have different types.
Name   <- c("Ben", "Alice", "Daniel", "Charlie")
Year   <- c(1990, 1992, 1995, 1993)
Option <- c("Biology", "Physics", "Chemistry", "Mathematics")

df <- data.frame(First_Name = Name, Year = Year, Options = Option)

# Accessing columns
df$Year           # 1990 1992 1995 1993
df[["Year"]]      # same
df[, 2]           # same — all rows, column 2

# Accessing elements
df$Options[3]     # "Chemistry"
df[2:3, 3]        # "Physics" "Chemistry"

# Merging two dataframes
Full_Names <- data.frame(First_Name = c("Alice","Ben"),
                         Last_Name  = c("Parker","James"))

merge(df, Full_Names)          # Inner join — only matching rows
merge(df, Full_Names, all=TRUE) # Outer join — all rows, NA for missing



Function
What it does


data.frame(...)
Create a dataframe from named vectors


as.data.frame(X)
Convert a matrix to a dataframe


dim(df)
Rows and columns


colnames(df)
Column names


str(df)
Structure overview (types, first values)


merge(a, b)
Join two dataframes on shared columns

title: Basics in Coding
text:
Loops & Iteration

apply family & for loops
Mat <- matrix(rnorm(12), nrow = 3)

apply(Mat, 1, mean)   # mean of each ROW    (MARGIN = 1)
apply(Mat, 2, mean)   # mean of each COLUMN (MARGIN = 2)

x <- c(1:5)
sapply(x, sqrt)       # apply sqrt() to each element → returns vector
lapply(x, sqrt)       # same but returns a list

# For loop
for (i in 1:4) {
  print(i * 3)
}

# If / else
a <- 5; b <- 10
if (a < b) { print("a is smaller") } else { print("b is smaller") }



Function
What it does


apply(X, 1, fun)
Apply fun to each row of matrix/dataframe


apply(X, 2, fun)
Apply fun to each column


sapply(x, fun)
Apply fun to each element of vector/list → vector


lapply(x, fun)
Apply fun to each element → list

title: Basics in Coding
text:
Index Selection

which, %in%, is.na
x <- c(2, 8, 3, 7, 1)

which(x > 5)          # c(2, 4)  — INDICES where condition is TRUE
x[which(x > 5)]       # c(8, 7)  — VALUES at those indices

c("a","b","c") %in% c("b","d")  # FALSE TRUE FALSE
                                 # — is each element in the right-hand set?

is.na(c(1, NA, 3))    # FALSE TRUE FALSE
sum(is.na(x))         # count of NA values



Function / Operator
What it does


which(condition)
Returns indices where condition is TRUE


x %in% y
For each element of x: is it anywhere in y?


is.na(x)
TRUE for each NA element


na.omit(x)
Remove NA values from a vector or dataframe

title: Basics in Coding
text:
Variables & Assignments

Assigning values
Use = to assign a value to a variable. Python is case-sensitive — hello and Hello are different objects. There is no <- operator in Python.
a    = 2              # integer
b    = True           # boolean  (note capital T)
name = "Rosalinde"   # string

a + 3                # 5
print(name)          # Rosalinde



Function
What it does


type(x)
Show the type of x


dir()
List all names in the current scope


del x
Remove variable x

title: Basics in Coding
text:
Lists

Creating & accessing lists (R: vectors)
Python lists use 0-based indexing and can hold mixed types. Use [ ] for indexing and slicing.
y = [9, 3, 7, 2]    # list of length 4
len(y)               # 4

# Indexing (0-based!)
y[2]                 # 7        — third element (index 2)
y[1:3]               # [3, 7]   — elements at index 1 and 2
y[:-1]               # [9,3,7]  — all except last

# Filter with list comprehension
[x for x in y if x < 5]      # [3, 2]
[x < 5 for x in y]           # [False, True, False, True]
sum(x < 5 for x in y)        # 2  — count matching

# Modifying
y[0] = 10            # replace first element (index 0)

  Mixed types: Unlike R vectors, Python lists allow mixed types:
  [True, "hello", 3] stays as-is — no automatic conversion.
  Indexing starts at 0, not 1.

title: Basics in Coding
text:
NumPy Arrays

Creating & accessing arrays (R: matrices)
NumPy arrays are the Python equivalent of R matrices. Requires import numpy as np. Indexing is 0-based.
import numpy as np

X = np.array([[1, 2, 3],
              [4, 5, 6]])
# Shape: (2, 3)

X.shape          # (2, 3)  — rows, then columns
X[0, 1]          # 2       — row 0, column 1 (0-based!)
X[1, :]          # [4 5 6] — entire second row
X[:, 0]          # [1 4]   — entire first column

# Building from vectors
A = np.column_stack(([1,2], [3,4], [5,6]))  # join as columns

text:
Dictionaries

Creating & accessing dicts (R: lists)
Dictionaries hold key–value pairs of any type. Use [ ] with the key to access values — there is no $ or [[ ]] in Python.
L = {"color": ["blue", "red"], "size": 5, "active": True}

# Accessing content
L["color"]           # ["blue", "red"]
L["color"][1]        # "red"   — second element (0-based)

# Check if key exists
"color" in L         # True

# Modifying & deleting
L["size"] = 10       # change a value
L["new"]  = "hi"     # add a new key
del L["size"]        # delete a key

  R vs Python: R's L[["color"]] → Python's L["color"].
  Square brackets always return the value directly in Python — no double-bracket distinction.

DataFrames

Creating & accessing DataFrames (R: data.frame)
Pandas DataFrames are the Python equivalent of R dataframes. Requires import pandas as pd.
import pandas as pd

Name   = ["Ben", "Alice", "Daniel", "Charlie"]
Year   = [1990, 1992, 1995, 1993]
Option = ["Biology", "Physics", "Chemistry", "Mathematics"]

df = pd.DataFrame({"First_Name": Name, "Year": Year, "Options": Option})

# Accessing columns
df["Year"]            # Series: 1990 1992 1995 1993
df.Year               # same — attribute-style access
df.iloc[:, 1]         # same — all rows, column index 1 (0-based)

# Accessing elements
df["Options"].iloc[2]    # "Chemistry"
df.iloc[1:3, 2]          # "Physics", "Chemistry"

# Merging two DataFrames
Full_Names = pd.DataFrame({"First_Name": ["Alice","Ben"],
                            "Last_Name":  ["Parker","James"]})

pd.merge(df, Full_Names)                    # Inner join — matching rows only
pd.merge(df, Full_Names, how="outer")       # Outer join — all rows, NaN for missing

Loops & Iteration

for loops, list comprehensions & numpy
import numpy as np

Mat = np.random.randn(3, 4)

np.mean(Mat, axis=0)        # mean of each COLUMN
np.mean(Mat, axis=1)        # mean of each ROW

x = list(range(1, 6))       # [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
[np.sqrt(i) for i in x]     # list comprehension — apply to each element
list(map(np.sqrt, x))        # same result with map()

# For loop
for i in range(1, 5):

# If / else
a = 5; b = 10
if a < b:

else:
    print("b is smaller")

np.where, in, pd.isna
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

x = np.array([2, 8, 3, 7, 1])

np.where(x > 5)          # (array([1, 3]),)  — INDICES where condition is TRUE
x[np.where(x > 5)]       # array([8, 7])     — VALUES at those indices
x[x > 5]                 # array([8, 7])     — direct boolean indexing (shortcut)

"a" in ["b", "d"]        # False  — membership test
["a" in ["b","d"], "b" in ["b","d"], "c" in ["b","d"]]  # [False, True, False]

pd.isna(pd.Series([1, None, 3]))   # [False, True, False]
np.isnan(x.astype(float))          # array of bool (for float arrays)
